chapter_theme: Pattinathar's Mummanikkovai on Thirukkazhumalam (Sirkazhi): the Lord who floated on the deluge and fed the child Sambandar the milk of knowledge is praised as the Full One beyond the Vedas and the inner faculties, and the poet makes the ruined room of his mind the Lord's bedchamber, counts every being that has been his parent or his food through endless wombs, and tells how grace turned the whirl of a blind man's road into the sight of the one true thing behind a painted wall. Short verses say the devotees' devotees outrank the gods, that the body is impurity entire, and that when flower, leaf and water fail the heart is offering enough.
structure_note: Twelve units in the three-metre rotation (agaval, venba, kalitthurai) chained by last word to first (ஆங்கே / அருளின், அதற்கு / ஆரண, கருப்பொருளே / கருமுதல்). The metre labels beside the ids are the previous unit's and unreliable. 850 and 852 are akam fragments in a companion's voice. A prose remark printed after 851 is an editor's note on a variant, not verse.

842.reading: With the Himalaya's daughter inseparable on one side like an emerald creeper on a coral mountain, with a face like a thousand suns rising from the waves, her young breasts, lotus face, crescent brow, red-lily mouth and lotus hands holding the pot of nectar, and her blue-lily eyes blooming with your splendour, you sat at the Lord's ease in Kazhumalam of the brahmins, which floated above the nagas' land when the upper worlds sank below and stood as the one support of the three worlds in the flood; and when the brahmin child who came with his father, at the toddling age, cried 'Mother' from hunger, she stood before him and gave him the ball of milk kneaded with the food of knowledge; and when the brahmin angrily asked who gave it, the boy pointed with his hand and said he would show him, 'the one with the earring, the one with the bull': there you appeared in grace.
842.nuance: The second half is the Sambandar legend told in the child's own words, தோடுடைய செவியன் and பீடுடைய பெம்மான் echoing his first Tevaram hymn; ஞான போனகம், the food of knowledge, names the milk as the source of his poetry. The Lord addressed throughout is the one who 'appeared' (வெளிப்பட்டருளினை), so the long praise of Uma leads to his epiphany, not hers.

843.reading: The sea of grace, the Lord of Pugali who is the mass of substance and the way called the love of me his servant: for those who love and worship with joined hands those who say 'the one with darkness in his throat', who among the heavenly beings is a match?
843.nuance: The ranking is of the devotees' devotees above the gods (அண்டத்தார்), the same descent as 818 and 833 in the Marudur kovai. அடியேன் அன்பு என்னும் ஆறு, the way called my love, makes the poet's love itself the Lord's path rather than his own act.

844.reading: Beyond the four Vedas, hard for Narayana and the four-faced one who resolved to know him, the Full One who fills the middle, our father, the Lord of Pugali, the cause of every world, the core thing beyond the inner faculties.
844.nuance: பூரணன் and கருப்பொருள் are the two names the verse adds to the usual list: the Lord is the Full One and the kernel beyond the antahkarana (mind, intellect, will, ego). Pattinathar uses பூரணம் as a name of the Lord here as throughout his Pooranamalai; the medical Siddhars make it a technical term.

845.reading: The rubbish of impurity called lust, anger and the great lie had lain without end since the embryo began, through all my long days; with difficulty I scorned and cleared it, untied and drove off the five rutting buffaloes of dark killing anger, swept with love, lit the lamp of grace, left the darkness of sorrow, spread the canopy of truth in front, made the ruined room of my mind, which had lain in flimsy baseness, your bedchamber, and set you on the cushion of the mind's full lotus flower; Lord of Pugali who floated high as the raft on which the gods were saved when the first flood spread over the long earth and the burning sky and the two lights floated like foam and the wind tore up the mountains and Vishnu and Brahma and the gods trembled that this was the end, Pralaya-vidangar whom the Kaveri's dawn pours forth: with your rich anklets sounding softly, bringing the Himalaya's shoot with you in the sight that never cloys, you may deign to come here, my Lord.
845.nuance: The housework allegory matches the farming one at 821: lust and lies are rubbish, the senses are five buffaloes to be untied and driven out, love is the broom, grace the lamp, truth the canopy, and the Lord is invited to a bed, not a shrine. The invitation includes Uma (இமயக் கொழுந்தையும் உடனே கொண்டு), so the heart is to house the half-woman form of 842.

846.reading: Bearing the deer and the axe, the darkness that lives in his holy throat and the crescent, he who appeared on the flood for the gods and sat enthroned at Kazhumalam has stood in my heart as light.
846.nuance: The three stations of the Lord, the flood, the town and the heart, are one sentence, so the shrine's founding legend ends inside the poet. The chain word ஒளி is taken up by 847.

847.reading: How the light came, so that the darkness in my false mind left; how my inner flood cleared; how it came and grew sweet; how an unthought joy came; how love came; how clarity came at the last hour: that is the sweet grace of the dwellers in Kazhumalam.
847.nuance: Six exclamations of வந்தவா (how it came) list the stages of grace as received, light, clarity, sweetness, joy, love, clarity again, with no act of the poet's among them. கடைசார் அமையத்து is read as the last hour of life; it could be the final stage of the sequence.

848.reading: Ripe sweet fruit of grace, unceasing joy, love that does not end, sea of nectar to your devotees, Lord of Kazhumalam whose tall gold tower-tops split the clouds' bellies, supreme yogi who sits with the maiden of young breasts, I will tell you one thing: Father, from the day you first thought that all worlds and endless wombs and all things should appear, through so many wombs of unthinkable difference, there is no one and nothing that has not come as my mother and my father, one by one, and none that have not come as those whose father and mother I was; there is no ground where I was not born before, nor any where I did not die; there are no lives that have not eaten me, nor any that I have not eaten; all that time has gone; I, the dog, cannot weary myself any further. I have not learned the tantra that recites your five letters, light of the sky, nor consorted with those who learned it; even so, in one moment that was possible, taking the flower I placed as the flower and the word I spoke as the mantra, it is your duty to keep me from falling into the sea of the two, troublesome birth and death.
848.nuance: The kinship argument is complete in both directions, every being has parented him and he every being, and extended to eating and being eaten, so rebirth makes the whole world one family and one food-chain; the poet draws from it only exhaustion. The plea's logic is that the single flower and word, offered without training, must count as the ritual (சொன்னதும் மந்திரமாக), and that keeping him out is the Lord's debt (நின் கடனே).

849.reading: Those who do not worship with joined hands the Kazhumalam of the three-eyed Lord sink to their feet in the sea called lust and suffer, knowing no means to conquer it: they are those who do not consider that the body is impurity entire.
849.nuance: உடலாம் முழுமலத்தை ஓர்கிலார் makes the body not merely impure but the whole of impurity, and makes failing to see this the cause of lust and of not worshipping. The venba thus gives the dissection of 824 its doctrine.

850.reading: This girl worships; this girl loses her bangles; for her distress alone the gossip rises; what is one to do about what is rising? If she has seen with her own hands, so to speak, the unwashed gem that sits in my heart, the Lord of Kazhumalam, the axe-bearer, and come back, there is no blame in it at all.
850.nuance: An akam fragment in a companion's or mother's voice about the girl love-sick for the Lord: loosened bangles and public talk (அலர்) are the stock signs. கழுவா மணி puns on கழுமலம், the gem that needs no washing, the Lord already in the heart; who speaks the last clause and whether the seeing is a vision or a temple visit is not settled.

851.reading: After praising the Lord of Pugali whose fame shone in the twelve ages past under different names, the bull-rider, husband of Uma, who bent the mountain and burnt the three cities of the strong-shouldered demons, with young moon on his growing hair and the single eye in his forehead that glared at Kama, the beginning the gods do not know, the poet confesses: in my untaught heart base understanding followed me, and with the empty gaze that looks and forgets, each time I looked, everything everywhere, mine and others', the many that come to be and the many that perish, what goes, comes and passes, more numerous than the sand heaped in the clear-watered world, the non-existent seeming to be and the existent unseen, I lay for many days in darkness; and the way it shook me was like a man who cannot see with his eyes and reels, the pit becoming his road and the road a pit, stumbling without end from one into the other; so it came, until I gained by compassion your look of growing grace, and then everything appeared false to me and you alone, the rare one, appeared true: like the many carved and painted shapes a master painter drew to catch a likeness, which to those who run their hands over them all without stopping show themselves as one wall.
851.nuance: Two images carry the verse: the blind man for whom pit and road exchange places, which is the unenlightened state, and the painted wall, which is the enlightened one: the painter's many figures differ to the eye but the hand that feels them finds one surface, so the many things are false and the one substrate true. இல்லன உளவாய் உள்ளன காணா is the plain statement of maya in the Vedantic sense. The prose line printed after the verse (சடமாகிய உடம்பு எனக் கொண்டு, கல்லா உடம்பு எனவும் பாடமோதுவர்) is an editor's note that some read கல்லா உடம்பு for கல்லா உளத்தின்.

852.reading: So she rose; what will she do? Still she says 'show me the angry bull'; the konrai blossom of the Lord of flowery Pugali, on whose matted crown the serpents stretch and rise in swift anger.
852.nuance: The second akam fragment: the girl rises wanting the Lord's konrai garland, the lover's gift of love poetry. சினவேறு காட்டுதிர் என்னும் may be her plea to be shown the bull, that is the Lord, or the companions' refusal; the venba is elliptical and the subject of பாம்பு கலியா நிமிரும் (the serpents in the hair rising) may be a figure for her agitation as much as the Lord's ornament.

853.reading: If no flower is to be had, there is the green leaf; if no leaf, there is water everywhere; if nothing at all is to be had, there is the heart, today: so say these, as equal, for reaching the lotus feet, which not even the bee's pollen attains, of the Lord of southern Thonipuram who shares his body with the one of incomparable breasts.
853.nuance: The descending list, flower, leaf, water, heart, declares them equal offerings (இணையாகச் செப்பும்), so the heart is not a substitute but the same thing. இன்றே, today, refuses deferral. The last word, சார்வதற்கே, chains the kovai's end to its beginning (திரு / திருவளர்) and its claim closes the thought begun at Marudur 812.

links.note: Pattinathar uses பூரணன், the Full One, as a name of the Lord beyond the Vedas and the inner faculties; Agasthiyar says that those who call pooranam God must say what pooranam is and defines it as the sixteen kalas guarded in the body. The medical Siddhar turns the devotional epithet into a technical term, so his verse qualifies Pattinathar's usage rather than contradicting it.

Tirumular makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the mouth the gate and the senses the lamps; Pattinathar makes the mind a room swept with love and lit with the lamp of grace and the Lord's bedchamber. Both house the Lord in the person, but Tirumular's senses become lamps while Pattinathar's five buffaloes are driven out.

The Marudur agaval farms the heart and this one cleans it, with the same stages: deceit or lust removed first, love laid down, truth as manure or canopy, the five senses as cattle to be fenced out or buffaloes to be driven off, grace as the sprout or the lamp. In 821 the Lord is the fruit that grows; in 845 he is the guest invited in.

At Marudur the poet counts the endless wombs and the threefold pain of birth, bearing and death and asks for the thought to cross; at Kazhumalam he counts what the wombs have made of the world, every being his parent and his child, his eater and his food, and asks the Lord to take one flower and one word as the whole rite. The weariness is the same; the second verse widens the family and lowers the price.

Tirumular says he once held the body to be a thing of shame, then found the true substance within it and now cherishes it as the Highest One's temple; Pattinathar says those who do not know the body as impurity entire are the ones who sink in lust and do not worship. The conflict holds if Pattinathar's முழுமலம் is a doctrine about the body and not only a cure for lust; Tirumular's verse was written against exactly that doctrine.

824 lists what the body is, hair, skin, wound, blood, bone, marrow, slime, worms, excrement, nerves and disease, and finds no self in it; 849 states the conclusion, the body is impurity entire, and makes not seeing this the root of lust. The agaval gives the evidence and the venba the thesis.

Tirumular compares the soul striving by its deeds in its three states to a blind man whose eyes are open, who sees only the step ahead and feels his way with a stick; Pattinathar's unenlightened self is a man who cannot see, for whom the pit becomes the road and the road the pit, stumbling from one to the other. Tirumular's blind man still finds his way; Pattinathar's is only released by the Lord's look.

Tirumular says anyone can give a green leaf to God, grass to a cow, a mouthful to another and a kind word; Pattinathar says if there is no flower the leaf will do, if no leaf then water, and if nothing then the heart. Both make the smallest offering sufficient; Pattinathar goes one step further and makes the heart alone enough.

The Marudur kovai opens by saying the Lord gives release even to devotees who offer a green leaf; the Kazhumalam kovai closes by saying that when even the leaf and water fail, the heart is an equal offering. The two kovais frame one claim, that grace is not priced by the offering.

source_issues: 851 ends with a prose line, சடமாகிய வுடம்பெனக்கொண்டு, கல்லா வுடம்பெனவும் பாடாமோதுவர், which is an editor's variant note printed as if it were verse.
The metre labels beside the ids carry over the previous unit's metre (843, 846, 849, 852 are venbas; 844, 847, 850, 853 kalitthurais).
842 line 29 வேதியச்சிறுவன் and line 34 தோஒடுடைய / பீஇடுடைய use the alapedai spelling; 844 and 847 are printed without word spaces so segmentation is editorial.
